OrthoRef · Foot & Ankle · Midfoot & Forefoot

Midfoot & Forefoot Fractures

Navicular, cuboid and cuneiform injuries, the Lisfranc complex, metatarsals, sesamoids and phalanges — plus the crushed foot and foot compartment syndrome.

Sources: Rockwood & Green’s Fractures in Adults, 10th ed., Ch. 68 · AO Foundation Surgery Reference (marked AO)

IntroductionR&G 68

The midfoot runs from the Chopart joint line (calcaneocuboid + talocalcaneonavicular) to the Lisfranc joint line. Its five bones — navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms — are bound so tightly that isolated bony injury is rare, and a "simple" fracture should always prompt a search for a ligamentous injury.

~5%of foot injuries are midfoot
up to 30%of midfoot injuries missed or delayed
35%of foot fractures are metatarsal
~68%of metatarsal fractures are the 5th
30–50%of forefoot load on the 1st MT
Midfoot
Rare but often missed
Incidence 0.45% (5/100,000); mechanisms split equally between high and low energy. Missed or delayed injuries do worse than acutely treated ones.
Lisfranc
0.1–0.4% of fractures
Rising incidence (9.2–14 per 100,000 person-years), young men first. Pure ligamentous instability misdiagnosed in up to 20%.
Forefoot
Common, usually low energy
Metatarsals peak at 20–50 years; direct trauma is the commonest cause. Digital fractures are the commonest forefoot injury overall.
Crush
High-energy foot
Crush injury is the main risk factor for foot compartment syndrome; the "multiple injured foot" needs a staged approach.

Hansen’s joint hierarchy drives every reconstruction decision in this chapter: essential joints (talonavicular, 2nd–5th MTP) must be preserved; nonessential but useful joints (1st MTP, 4th/5th TMT) should be restored; nonessential joints (CC, 1st IP) may be temporarily transfixed; unnecessary joints (naviculocuneiform, 1st–3rd TMT, lesser PIP/DIP) may be fused or crossed by screws and plates.

A note on the 4th/5th TMT joints

The chapter lists the 4th and 5th TMT joints as "nonessential but useful" in the Hansen scheme, and later describes them as "essential joints" within the TMT complex because their mobility is important for normal foot function. Either way, the practical rule is the same: do not fuse the lateral column — a pseudarthrosis or interposition arthroplasty is preferred.

Clinical assessmentR&G 68

History
Energy and mechanism
Direct crush vs indirect axial/rotational load on a plantarflexed foot; sports twisting injuries are increasingly common.
Look
Plantar ecchymosis
Should raise suspicion of a TMT injury (though not always seen in isolated athletic injuries).
Feel
Tenderness by column
Medial column (navicular, cuneiforms, TMT-1/2) vs lateral column (CC, cuboid, TMT-4/5).
Soft tissues
Exclude compartment syndrome
Especially after crush; check for forefoot ischemia and blistering.

Provocative tests for TMT injury (Myerson & Cerrato)

  • TMT-1/2 squeeze test — transverse compression across the first and second rays.
  • Abduction–pronation maneuver — comparable to an apprehension test.
  • Inability to stand on tiptoe or bear weight pain-free; widening of the TMT transition zone compared with the other foot.
Beware the "sprained foot"

Pain seemingly out of proportion to the injury; beware a patient told in the emergency room they had a sprained foot. Up to 20% of Lisfranc fracture-dislocations are missed at initial evaluation AO.

ImagingR&G 68 · AO

Start with AP, lateral and oblique views; add weight-bearing or stress imaging whenever stability is in doubt, and obtain CT for any tarsal fracture — plain films detected only 33% of navicular fractures seen on CT.

ToolWhat it adds
AP / oblique / lateralBaseline for all injuries. R&G specifies the oblique in 30° internal rotation; AO specifies a 45° internal oblique AO.
Weight-bearing filmsDistinguish unstable ligamentous injury from sprain; NWB films are insufficient for this.
Stress fluoroscopyAbduction/adduction stress; more sensitive than WB films in cadaver work. Stødle: negative stress test → no progression to arthrosis.
CTKey tool for tarsal fractures; detects 60% more metatarsal and twice as many tarsal fractures than radiographs in high-energy injury; separates fleck sign from os intermetatarseum.
Weight-bearing CTSripanich: normal C1–M2 distance 3.9 mm; relative widening >1.5 mm under partial load suggests complete Lisfranc ligament injury.
MRIBest direct view of the Lisfranc ligament (sens 94%, spec 75% for instability, Raikin); first choice when films are normal but suspicion is high, or in chronic cases.
Bone scanLargely replaced by MRI; high sensitivity for stage I athletic injuries (Nunley–Vertullo).

Radiographic alignment rules at the TMT line

AP
TMT-1
Lateral border of the medial cuneiform in line with the lateral border of the 1st MT base.
AP
TMT-2
Medial margin of the 2nd MT base colinear with the intermediate cuneiform — the key AP indicator.
Oblique
TMT-3 / TMT-4
Medial border of the 3rd MT with the lateral cuneiform; medial border of the 4th MT with the cuboid (key oblique indicator).
Lateral
Dorsal cortices
Dorsal cortex of the metatarsals even with the dorsal cortex of the cuneiforms; step-off = dorsal displacement AO.

Malalignment of ≥1 mm is pathologic. Normal 1st/2nd intermetatarsal base distance on weight-bearing films averages 2.5 mm. The fleck sign (avulsion from the 2nd MT base or medial cuneiform) is pathognomonic for Lisfranc injury; the gap sign (widened intercuneiform distance) is pathognomonic for Lisfranc ligament rupture.

Medial column sign (Coss)

A tangent along the medial border of the medial cuneiform should intersect the 1st MT base. With forefoot abduction stress, a line passing medial to the base is a positive medial column sign — incompetence of the Lisfranc plus dorsal TMT ligaments.

More thresholds from the chapter
  • Bilateral WB films (multicentre): 2nd MT base–intermediate cuneiform malalignment ≥0.3 mm = high sensitivity; 2nd MT base–medial cuneiform distance ≥2.1 mm = high specificity.
  • Any 1st/2nd MT base diastasis >2 mm on an AP foot film should raise suspicion of Lisfranc ligament injury.
  • 5th MT: Ottawa Foot Rules are 100% sensitive and 79% specific; if films are normal but the base is tender, an AP ankle film including the proximal 5th MT can show a tuberosity tip avulsion.
  • Sesamoids: add an axial (skyline) view; bipartite sesamoids have smooth edges, fractures are irregular.
  • Bipartite medial cuneiform (0.79% on MRI) cleaves horizontally; acute fractures usually cleave coronally.
  • Weight-bearing, stress and CT are hard to obtain acutely; serial radiographs are needed to detect further displacement.

Columns, arches and ligamentsR&G 68

Think of the midfoot as a rigid medial column (navicular as keystone) and a mobile lateral column (cuboid as keystone), linked by the cuneiforms into a transverse "Roman" arch.

Ligaments
Plantar > dorsal
Plantar ligaments are stronger (repetitive gait loading) — so dislocations are usually dorsal.
Lateral
Bifurcate ligament
Anterior calcaneal process to cuboid and lateral navicular.
Medial
Spring ligament complex
Plantar calcaneonavicular, dorsal talonavicular and medial calcaneonavicular ligaments.
Dynamic
Tibialis posterior
Only tendon inserting entirely in the midfoot; interlocks the bones into a rigid lever at midstance and toe-off.
TMT columnJointsSagittal motion
MedialTMT-1 (ellipsoid)Up to 3.5 mm; no 1st–2nd intermetatarsal ligament
IntermediateTMT-2, TMT-3 (flat)0.6 mm (TMT-2), 1.6 mm (TMT-3) — most stable
LateralTMT-4, TMT-59.6 mm and 10.2 mm — shock absorbers after heel strike

The Lisfranc complexR&G 68

The 2nd metatarsal base is the keystone: recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms by a short intermediate cuneiform, it gives the TMT line its bony stability.

Interosseous
Lisfranc ligament
Lateral surface of the medial cuneiform → lower medial 2nd MT base. Thick band; largest TMT ligament; >2× load-to-failure and stiffness of the dorsal ligament.
Plantar
Plantar Lisfranc (pC1-M2M3)
Strongest plantar ligament; two bands to the 2nd and 3rd MT bases. Disruption predicts instability on MRI.
Dorsal
Weakest bundle
Fails first under axial load on a plantarflexed foot → dorsal displacement.
Lateral plantar
Newly described
5th MT base + lateral cuneiform → plantar 2nd MT base, in 62% of cadavers; may explain spontaneous reduction of TMT-4/5 after TMT-1/2 are reduced.
No 1st–2nd or 4th cuneometatarsal interosseous ligament

There are no interosseous TMT ligaments between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals, or in the space formed by MT-4/5 and the cuboid. The Lisfranc complex is also supported from below by a lattice of tibialis posterior, peroneus longus and FHL.

Midfoot bonesR&G 68

Tarsal bone anatomyAnatomy explorer
Medial column keystone
Tarsal navicular
  • Proximal concave TN articulation — an essential joint, ~37° of motion, much of sagittal midfoot motion.
  • Distal convex facets to the three cuneiforms = unnecessary joints; inconsistent cuboid facet.
  • Only tendon insertion: anterior portion of tibialis posterior (medial).
  • Blood supply from dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial branches via the medial pole, dorsal and plantar surfaces; relatively avascular central third (though McKeon found no avascular zone in 58.8% of specimens).
  • Incomplete navicular–calcaneal coalition in 1%.
Lateral column keystone
Cuboid
  • Only bone of the lateral midfoot; articulates with calcaneus, navicular, lateral cuneiform, and MT-4/5.
  • Maintains lateral column length and contributes to midtarsal/TMT motion and CC pronation–supination.
  • Protected between calcaneus and 4th/5th MT bases — but displaced fractures need articular reconstruction and length restoration.
Transverse arch
Medial, intermediate, lateral cuneiforms
  • Apex of the transverse arch is the intermediate cuneiform — the smallest and inversely wedged.
  • Medial cuneiform: tibialis anterior (inferoposterior medial surface), peroneus longus (plantar), origin of the Lisfranc ligament.
  • Lateral cuneiform: most variable (uncinate process, coalitions).
  • Dimensions (height × width): medial 32.6 × 14.1 mm; intermediate 23.1 × 9.6 mm; lateral 23.4 × 10.9 mm; whole complex 44.7 mm wide.

Forefoot bonesR&G 68

1st MT
Short, wide, independent
Tibialis anterior (plantar-medial base) elevates the head; peroneus longus (plantar-lateral base) plantarflexes it. Highest peak pressures during most activities.
2nd/3rd MT
Rigid keystone rays
Immobile at the cuneiforms — which is why stress fractures concentrate here. Flexors pull the distal fragment plantar and proximal.
4th MT
Least injured central
Protected by position and lateral ray flexibility.
Transverse MT ligament
Distal tether
Links the plantar plates of adjacent MTPs.

Fifth metatarsal

  • Insertions: peroneus brevis (dorsolateral tubercle), peroneus tertius (dorsal metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction), abductor digiti quinti (plantar groove), lateral band of the plantar fascia (plantar tubercle).
  • Three proximal articulations: cuboid–5th MT, cuboid–4th MT, 4th–5th MT.
  • Mimics: adolescent tuberosity apophysis; os peroneum (in peroneus longus at the lateral cuboid) and os vesalianum (proximal to the base, medial to peroneus brevis) — smooth contours.

The shaft is fed by a single nutrient artery entering the medial cortex at the proximal–middle third junction; the base and tuberosity by metaphyseal and epiphyseal vessels. The metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction is a watershed — the leading explanation for delayed union and nonunion of proximal 5th MT fractures.

Hallucal sesamoids

  • Within the two heads of FHB, joined by the intersesamoid ligament (core of the 1st MTP plantar plate); protect the FHL tendon.
  • Transmit up to 50% of body weight, ~300% at push-off. Tibial (medial) sesamoid is larger and more often injured.
  • Each has a single artery entering proximally and plantarly → distal poles poorly vascularized; dorsal or medial approaches are safer.
  • Tibial sesamoid bipartite in up to 30% — bilateral in 80–90% of these; fibular rarely bipartite.

Compartments of the footR&G 68

Nine compartments are distinguished experimentally (ten on MRI). The dorsal compartment continues the anterior leg compartment; the plantar compartments communicate with the deep posterior leg compartment through the tarsal tunnels — so leg and foot compartment syndromes can coexist.

CompartmentContentsNeedle landmark / depth
MedialAbductor hallucis, FHB; medial plantar a/n~6 cm below medial malleolus, ~11 mm
LateralADM, FDMB, opponens; lateral plantar a/n~11 cm along malleolus–5th MT head line, ~11 mm
Central superficialFDB, lumbricals, FDL tendons~11.5 cm from plantar fat pad insertion, ~10 mm
Central deep (adductor)Adductor hallucis, oblique headSame entry, ~21 mm
Central intermediate (calcaneal)Quadratus plantae; lateral plantar a; medial/lateral plantar n~6 cm from medial malleolus, ~24 mm — the most sensitive compartment
Interosseous ×4Plantar/dorsal interosseiDorsal, between MTs, ~10–12 mm; 13–15 cm from medial malleolus

PrinciplesR&G 68

No midfoot or forefoot classification reliably guides treatment or predicts outcome. The chapter’s treatment logic instead rests on three questions: displaced or not, is the column stable, and isolated or multiple/bicolumn injury.

RegionOTA/AO code
Navicular83 (A noncomminuted, B comminuted)
Cuboid84 (A avulsion, B partial articular, C complete articular)
Cuneiforms85.1 / 85.2 / 85.3 (medial / middle / lateral)
Midfoot dislocations80-C / 80-D (see note)
Metatarsals87 (segment 1 proximal, 2 diaphysis, 3 distal)
Phalanges88
Crush / multiple fractures89-B
Note on dislocation codes

The navicular section codes midfoot dislocations as 80-C (TN 80-C1, NC 80-C3, multiple 80-C9); the cuneiform section of the same chapter codes them as 80-D (TN D1, CC D2, NC D3, intercuneiform D4, TMT D5 with D5.1–D5.6, multiple D6). Both are shown as printed; direction of dislocation is not coded in either.

NavicularR&G 68

Navicular fracturesClassification explorer
Most common
Avulsion (flake) fracture
  • TN or naviculocuneiform ligament avulsions, often with capsuloligamentous tears.
  • Mostly nonoperative; larger fragments involving articular surface → operative.
Traction injury
Tuberosity fracture
  • Tibialis posterior insertion avulsed without joint disruption — e.g., valgus "nutcracker" mechanism.
Sangeorzan I
Horizontal (dorsal/plantar)
  • Transverse split into dorsal and plantar segments with disruption of the dorsal ligaments.
Sangeorzan II
Vertical (medial/lateral)
  • Usually abduction injury; vertical fracture with lateral comminution and TN ligament disruption.
  • Split usually follows an intercuneiform line; stress fractures fall here.
Sangeorzan III
Comminuted
  • Severe axial load with abduction and plantarflexion; CC joint and NC ligaments frequently involved.
  • Central comminution → loss of medial arch height and medial column shortening.
Revised system
Schmid I–III
  • I single fracture line; II any comminution; III any TN dislocation or talar head lesion.
  • Correlated with outcome scores and TN arthritis (Sangeorzan did not).
  • Sanders: type II did better with a tension-band plate than a screw; type III did poorly, needed multiple surgeries, often developed arthritis — consider primary TN fusion.
14% of stress fractures
Navicular stress fracture
  • Partial or complete; start mid-dorsally and progress plantarward.
  • Risk factors: long 2nd/short 1st ray, pes cavus, metatarsus adductus, equinus, limited subtalar motion, training errors.
  • Suspected → MRI or 1-mm CT perpendicular to the navicular. 96% healed nonoperatively (meta-analysis).
OTA/AO navicular (83) figure

CuboidR&G 68

Cuboid fractures (Fenton)Classification explorer
Fenton I
CC capsular avulsion
  • Simple avulsion of the CC joint capsule. Avulsions are the commonest cuboid injury (50–70%), often with a sprain; ~70% missed initially.
Fenton II
Extra-articular body
  • Isolated extra-articular fracture of the cuboid body.
Fenton III
Intra-articular body
  • Intra-articular fracture confined to the cuboid.
Fenton IV
With midfoot/TMT disruption
  • Associated disruption of the midfoot and TMT injuries.
Fenton V
Midtarsal + column crush
  • Mid-tarsal disruption with crushing of the lateral column alone or both columns.
Older systems
Sangeorzan–Swiontkowski · Weber–Locher
  • Sangeorzan: crush, proximal articular, distal articular, combined.
  • Weber–Locher: distal cubometatarsal extension (dorsolateral or plantar-lateral wall) vs burst with column shortening; no extra-articular type described.
Nutcracker and cuboid syndrome
  • Nutcracker fracture: indirect abduction mechanism; sudden pain and inability to weight bear. Court-Brown: cuboid fractures were lower energy and commoner in older women; men had higher-energy injuries and more navicular fractures.
  • Cuboid syndrome: painful cuboid subluxation, ~18% of ballet dancers; reduced Chopart mobility; the "cuboid squeeze" (Marshall) reduces it; conservative care usually returns full function.

CuneiformsR&G 68

Choi typePattern
IAExtra-articular avulsion (chip or shell-like cortical)
IBIntra-articular avulsion
IIAxial compression
IIIDirect blow to the dorsum

Treatment of cuneiform injuries is based on instability or shortening, not fracture pattern. Stress injuries on MRI in military personnel: medial 9.5%, intermediate 6.9%, lateral 4.5%.

Tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc)R&G 68

Quénu and Küss (1909) described homolateral, isolated and divergent patterns; Hardcastle and Myerson refined them by congruity and direction. None adequately represents pure ligamentous or nondisplaced injuries.

Myerson classificationClassification explorer
Total incongruity
Type A — complete
  • Complete incongruity of the whole TMT line in any plane or direction (homolateral).
Partial incongruity
Type B1 — partial medial
  • Partial incongruity involving the first ray.
Partial incongruity
Type B2 — partial lateral
  • Dislocation of one or more of the lateral four metatarsals.
Divergent
Type C1 — partial divergent
  • First ray medialized with dislocation and partial incongruity of the lateral metatarsals.
Divergent
Type C2 — total divergent
  • Divergent pattern with complete incongruity.
Low-energy athletic
Stages I–III
StageFindings
ISprain; no diastasis on WB films; positive bone scan
II1st/2nd diastasis 1–5 mm; no loss of arch height
IIIDiastasis >5 mm with loss of medial column height

MetatarsalsR&G 68

OTA/AO 87, analogous to the metacarpals: metatarsal identifier, then segment (1 proximal, 2 diaphysis, 3 distal); A extra-articular/simple, B partial articular/wedge, C complete articular/multifragmentary. It describes the pattern but gives no guide to stability or treatment. By region: proximal metaphyseal/base fractures stay aligned (but may signal Lisfranc injury); diaphyseal fractures are often oblique and shorten; distal metaphyseal fractures displace plantar and lateral.

Proximal fifth metatarsal

Proximal 5th MT (Lawrence–Botte)Classification explorer
46–73%
Tuberosity avulsion
  • Sudden hindfoot inversion; tension via the lateral band of the plantar aponeurosis (peroneus brevis may displace it further).
  • May be comminuted or enter the cuboid facet.
  • Pettersen 2022: 61.2% of 834 fractures.
14–39%
True Jones fracture
  • Acute forefoot adduction; tensile fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, propagating toward the 4th–5th articulation.
  • Long, narrow, straight 5th MT with adducted forefoot may be at higher risk.
  • Pettersen 2022: 18.8%.
8–15%
Proximal diaphyseal stress fracture
  • Within the proximal 1.5 cm of the shaft; athletes; repetitive tensile load starting at the lateral cortex.
  • Prodromal symptoms; tendency to nonunion.
  • Pettersen 2022: 20.0%.
Healing status
Torg I–III
TypeFindings
I — acuteNo prior symptoms; narrow fracture line
II — delayed unionPrior trauma, periosteal reaction, widened line, radiolucency
III — nonunionRepetitive trauma, periosteal bone, sclerotic medullary canal
"Dancer’s fracture"
Spiral diaphyseal fracture
  • Rotational force on an axially loaded plantarflexed foot (rolling over the lateral border); spiral from distal-lateral to proximal-medial.
  • Increasingly seen in women over 40 after low-energy trauma — consider a metabolic work-up as an early fragility fracture.
  • Neck fractures ~6.7% of 5th MT fractures.
Terminology clash — "Jones"

R&G uses Jones for the zone 2 metaphyseal–diaphyseal fracture. AO Surgery Reference labels proximal articular 5th MT fractures "Jones fracture", proximal extra-articular fractures "march fracture", and proximal avulsions "pseudo-Jones" AO. Check which convention a source uses. A survey found 70% of AOFAS members treat zones 2 and 3 the same way, and a two-zone system has high interrater reliability.

Sesamoids and phalangesR&G 68

Sesamoid
Acute vs stress
Simple vs stellate (comminuted, higher osteonecrosis risk). Sesamoid stress fractures are 1–3% of all stress fractures.
Phalanx
OTA/AO 88
Toe identifier (T hallux, N, M, R, L), then proximal (1), middle (2), distal (3) phalanx; A extra-articular, B partial articular/wedge, C complex. No proven value for treatment or prognosis.

The multiple injured footR&G 68

  • Zwipp: one point per involved functional level (5 levels) + soft-tissue grade up to 4 (degloving, subtotal amputation, crushed foot). A sum ≥5 = "complex trauma of the foot". Describes severity but has no prognostic value and should not decide amputation.
  • Hidalgo–Shaw: I soft-tissue loss <3 cm² without bone injury; II >3 cm² without bone injury; III with osseous involvement (staged debridement, fixation, flap).
  • Jeng (plantar avulsions): suprafascial → defat and full-thickness graft; subfascial proximally based → suture back; distally based → revascularize if possible.
  • MESS and Hannover scores were built for the leg and do not apply to the foot.
NavicularCuboidCuneiformLisfranc1st MTCentral MT5th MTSesamoidPhalanxHigh energy

For every tarsal fracture the authors ask the same three questions: (1) displaced vs nondisplaced, (2) is the column stable (dynamic fluoroscopy / weight-bearing films), and (3) isolated vs multiple or bicolumn injury. Soft tissues come first: open fractures need immediate debridement, compartment syndrome immediate decompression, and severely contused skin closed reduction with K-wires.

Cuboid<2 mm, lateral column intact; avulsions≥2 mm; articular incongruity >1 mm; shortening; lateral column instability
Cuneiform<2 mm, isolated, stable columnDisplacement; instability; multiple cuneiform/midfoot fractures
TMTMalalignment <1 mm, articular <2 mm, stable on stressMalalignment ≥1 mm; articular >2 mm; C1–M1 >4 mm; instability vs other side

Navicular fracturesR&G 68

Nonoperative
Short-leg cast 6–8 wk
No or toe-touch weight bearing; recheck stability with WB films or stress fluoroscopy at 1–2 weeks. Any doubt → ORIF.
Stress fracture
NWB cast 6–8 wk
Outcomes equal to surgery (Torg meta-analysis); surgery may allow earlier return to sport (Mallee).
ORIF
Gold standard if displaced
Tenets: restore medial column length and the TN articular surface.
Primary fusion
Salvage
Bone loss >40% → TN fusion suggested; NC fusion preserves TN motion. Authors: primary arthrodesis gives unsatisfactory results with more nonunion.
Why nonoperative care of combined injuries fails

Howie: 5 of 14 patients with navicular fractures and associated lateral column injuries had poor results, with 80% secondary arthritis — instability, not the fracture, drives the outcome.

Postoperative course

0–6 wk
Boot or cast, NWB 6 weeks
6 & 10 wk
WB films; consider ex-fix / pin removal
6–8 wk
Vigorous out-of-boot mobilization of essential joints
10–12 wk
PWB → as tolerated if healing; CT if union unclear
12 wk
Remove spanning device at least across TN
Bone graft and adjunct external fixation — evidence
  • Grafting (iliac crest, proximal tibia; calcaneus or distal tibia locally) improved reduction quality but not convalescence or outcome (Coulibaly: 11 of 41 operated cases). Authors recommend autograft for comminution.
  • External fixation for ≥6 weeks restores length but not impacted articular zones; Chandran: 11 open midfoot injuries, removal at ~9 weeks, 2 pin-tract infections, pain in 6.
  • Richter: ex-fix used in 35.5% of 148 operated midfoot fractures; primary fusion needed in only 4.7%.

Cuboid fracturesR&G 68

Nonoperative
Short-leg cast, NWB 6–8 wk
Stable nondisplaced fractures (authors: walking cast 6–8 wk). Simple cortical avulsions: WBAT in a boot, elastic bandage or AFO.
Operative
Now favoured if displaced
Restore lateral column length and articular surface; compression fractures always shorten the column and usually need graft.
Dislocation
Rare
Axial traction + thumb pressure; peroneal tendon interposition may block reduction; transfix TMT-4/5 with K-wires 6–8 wk.
Fusion
Avoid at CMT-4/5
CC fusion is salvage; cuboid–4th/5th MT fusion is poorly tolerated → interposition arthroplasty (nonunion after arthrodesis up to 10.8%).
Operative indications as printed

Open fracture; displacement ≥2 mm; articular incongruity >1 mm; lateral column instability; multiple midfoot injuries; compartment syndrome; and shortening — listed in the chapter’s indications box as "shortening <3 mm".

0–2 wk
Padded splint/boot; sutures out at 2 wk
0–6 wk
NWB 6 weeks (except small avulsions)
6–12 wk
PWB → FWB; PT from 6–8 wk
10–12 wk
CT if union questionable
3–6 mo
Remove lateral bridge plate

Outcome: Weber–Locher (12 patients) — minor ROM loss in all, residual disability 75%, lateral pain 25%, early arthritis 25% with joint involvement. Rony (9 patients, fracture-specific locking plate): good alignment and scores at 4 years.

Cuneiform injuriesR&G 68

Only nondisplaced fractures with a stable medial column are treated nonoperatively (short-leg cast, NWB 6–8 weeks, close follow-up — secondary dislocation is common). Everything else needs fixation.

Nondisplaced · stable
Cast
NWB 6–8 weeks; WB films or stress exam first.
Nondisplaced · unstable or multiple
Percutaneous fixation
Higher risk of secondary loss of reduction.
Displaced · isolated · closed reduction works
Percutaneous pins/screws
1.6–2.0 mm pins or 2.7–3.5 mm screws.
Displaced · otherwise
ORIF
Longitudinal dorsal approach; free an interposed tibialis anterior.
  • Intercuneiform screws first, medial → lateral (2.7-mm cortical, countersunk) to build a stable medial block; then metatarsocuneiform or naviculocuneiform transfixation.
  • Never fix to the cuboid — it crosses the columns and blocks independent motion.
  • Graft voids (calcaneus, distal tibia); partial fusion with high injury severity. NWB 6 weeks; K-wires out at 6 weeks.

Tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) injuriesR&G 68 · AO

Stable injuries are treated in a cast; any instability — ligamentous or bony — is fixed. The key to outcome is anatomic alignment and articular congruity, especially of the medial column.

Nonoperative protocol (stable, nondisplaced)

0–6 wk
Below-knee cast, NWB; WB films every 2 weeks
6–12 wk
Toe-touch → progressive WB in cast/boot
12 wk
Final review; shoe modification, orthoses, arch support
≥4 mo
Rest from ladder, kneeling, running work
6–9 mo
Typical work/sport reintegration
Stødle
Excellent at 55 months
26 stable injuries (<2 mm displacement, negative stress test) treated nonoperatively; one radiologic OA at 1 year, none clinical at 5 years.
No stress test?
Half displace
Skipping stress radiography leads to further displacement in up to half of patients.
Athletes
94–96% return
Nonoperatively treated undisplaced / stable minimally displaced injuries returned to sport in 94% and 96% (two meta-analyses).

CRIF
Closed reduction, internal fixation
  • K-wire / 2.7-mm screw for the TMT injury; address the associated foot injury.
CRIF
Pure ligamentous instability
  • 1.6–2.0 mm K-wires, 2.7–3.5 mm screws — the reduction must still be anatomic, especially medially.
  • Myerson B and subtle unstable injuries: slightly (not significantly) better outcomes with percutaneous treatment.
ORIF
Simple extra-/intra-articular fracture
  • Medial: dorsomedial approach, 2.7/3.5 screws, spanning fixation or 2.0/2.7/tubular plates ± graft.
  • Lateral: dorsolateral approach, K-wires or screws, or internal spanning fixation.
ORIF
Comminuted extra-articular
  • Medial: plates + bone graft + adjunct external or internal spanning fixation.
  • Lateral: K-wires/screws or temporary internal/external spanning.
PA / ORIF
Comminuted articular
  • Medial: primary arthrodesis (plates or crossed 2.7/3.5 screws + graft).
  • Lateral: ORIF + temporary spanning — pseudarthrosis preferred over fusion.
  • Complete TMT fusion = salvage, staged medial then lateral.

ORIF vs primary arthrodesis

Meta-analysis
No outcome difference
389 ORIF vs 158 PA: similar clinical outcomes; ORIF had more hardware removal and secondary arthrodesis.
Henning · Ly
PA better function
PA gave better function at 24 and 42 months; Ly (ligamentous): participation 62→92% after ORIF, 44→65% after fusion.
Conflicting reviews
PA not inferior
Revision, reduction, infection, complications, satisfaction, VAS, return to work: no difference. Arthritis and unplanned return to OR higher after ORIF.
Timing
Within 4–6 weeks
After ~6 weeks deformity becomes fixed (Rammelt); delayed ORIF of missed low-energy TMT-1/2 injuries can still do acceptably.

Fusion indications proposed: destruction of >50% of the articular surface, or (1) major ligamentous disruption with multidirectional instability, (2) comminuted intra-articular fracture of a medial metatarsal base, (3) midfoot crush with intra-articular fracture-dislocation. The lateral column is never fused.

AO reconstruction sequence
  • 1. Cuneiforms ↔ navicular. 2. 2nd MT ↔ middle cuneiform — the reference for every other reduction. 3. 2nd MT ↔ medial cuneiform. 4. TMT-1, then 3, 4 and 5 AO.
  • 1st–3rd TMT bony injuries are reconstructed or fused; 4th–5th TMT stay mobile, usually with temporary K-wires AO.
  • Lisfranc injuries may be associated with compartment syndrome in more than 25% AO — R&G calls it uncommon but still recommends pressure measurement with marked swelling.
Day 0
Bivalved below-knee cast
0–6 wk
Short-leg cast, toe-touch
6–12 wk
Stepwise increase to FWB
12 wk
Remove problematic hardware; K-wires 6–12 wk, bridging ≥12 wk AO
≤1 yr
Supportive insoles; proprioception and calf/foot strength
Implant evidence (screws, plates, suture buttons)
  • Lisfranc screw failure ~157 N; no difference between C1→M2 and M2→C1 directions. Partially threaded cannulated = fully threaded solid.
  • Dorsal bridge plating ≈ screw stability in cadavers and avoids articular damage; Bansal: screws better resisted plantar diastasis.
  • Onochie: 85 dorsal bridge plates, 40 months, 8 fusions, only 21% plates removed (symptomatic, mostly female).
  • Suture button / tape constructs: similar stability to screws in isolated ligament transection (some studies favour screws); a tape with intercuneiform limb matched screws under high load (Koroneos).
  • Isolated TMT-2 lag screw arthrodesis inferior to two lag screws or lag screw + locking plate; adding TMT-1/3 fusion did not increase TMT-2 stability.
  • Routine removal may be unnecessary; some remove routinely in athletes at 4–6 months.

First metatarsal fracturesR&G 68 · AO

Only ~1.5% of metatarsal fractures, but the 1st ray carries the highest pressures. Stress radiographs decide: any instability or loss of head position needs fixation.

Nonoperative
Isolated, stable, minimal displacement
Short-leg cast NWB 3 weeks, then WBAT 3 weeks. Cast prone with knee at 90°, no dorsal pressure on the 1st MT.
ORIF
Unstable or displaced
Oblique/spiral → 2.7-mm lag screws; transverse or comminuted → one-third tubular or 2.7-mm plate (medial cuneiform to intact shaft if needed).
External fixation
Severe comminution / open
Pins in midfoot and proximal phalanx; phalanx at least plantigrade, ideally slightly dorsiflexed.
Fusion
Comminuted TMT-1
Comminuted intra-articular fracture-dislocation of TMT-1 → primary fusion.
Don’t dorsiflex the 1st MT

Approaching from dorsal, a dorsiflexed 1st MT creates a sagittal deformity and transfer lesions under the lesser heads. Push the sole with a flat surface and check AP, lateral and oblique fluoroscopy. AO: the sesamoids bear weight in the first ray, so check axial alignment at the sesamoid level AO.

Postoperative: short-leg cast (or removable splint for wound care), NWB 6–8 weeks, then boot; radiographs at 2, 6, 12 weeks and up to 1 year.

Central metatarsal fracturesR&G 68

Most isolated central MT fractures are stable and heal in a stiff-soled shoe. The treatment target is the metatarsal head position: dorsiflexed → transfer metatarsalgia; plantarflexed → plantar keratosis.

Correct any fracture with >10° sagittal angulation or 3–4 mm translation in any plane, any comminuted fracture, multiple adjacent fractures, and an unstable 2nd MT base (no 1st–2nd ligament to stop lateral drift; think Lisfranc).

Head/neck deviated
Closed reduction + pin
Distraction to realign, then pin. Multiple head/neck fractures: closed reduction under local — open surgery risks devascularizing the head.
Multiple adjacent
Fix at least one
Usually unstable; ORIF at least one MT (consider the 1st), then transverse pins from the length-stable ray.
Open reduction
Low-profile implants
Oblique → lag screw ± neutralization plate; transverse → plate or tension band; comminuted oblique → plate.
Outcomes
K-wires work
Zarei: 58 fractures, 1.5-mm K-wires, union 6.5 weeks, no nonunion, AOFAS 95.2. Bryant: 75 plated fractures, no nonunion.
Lateral drift of head fractures

Enter the proximal phalanx base or head from lateral and bend the pin down the medial wall of the shaft; the elastic bend pushes medially against the natural lateral drift.

0–2 wk
Splint/cast; heel weight bearing
2 wk
Sutures out → removable boot
4–6 wk
Comfortable weight bearing
6 wk
Pins out (unless bridging a gap)

Fifth metatarsal fracturesR&G 68 · AO

Treatment by zoneManagement explorer
Tuberosity avulsion
Mostly functional treatment
  • Stiff-soled shoe, boot, bandage or AFO with WBAT; heals in 3–12 weeks in nearly all.
  • Boot or bandage beats a short-leg cast (better function, fewer nonunions); hard-soled shoe beat cast in athletes (RCT).
  • Even displaced or intra-articular avulsions do well in nonathletes.
When to fix — three thresholds in the chapter
  • Athletes/young adults: percutaneous screw better when displaced >2–3 mm (RCT).
  • Authors’ text: displacement >5 mm → screw or tension band; in athletes any displacement.
  • Algorithm 68-7: involvement of >30% of the articular surface → ORIF with screw.
  • Screw beat tension band wiring; tiny fragments → tension band. Distal ulna hook plate: good results in 21.
Jones
Acute metaphyseal–diaphyseal
  • Nonathletes: short-leg NWB cast 6 weeks, then walker and progressive weight bearing; return to sport up to ~10 weeks.
  • Nonunion after nonoperative care reported up to 21%.
  • Athletes: operate — screw fixation union 95% vs 66% nonoperative; return to sport 98.4% at 9.7 vs 13.1 weeks.
  • Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound shows promise for incomplete stress (Jones) fractures.
Stress
Proximal diaphyseal stress fracture
  • Prodromal pain → NWB cast for an additional 8 weeks, then reassess (dissolving sclerosis, medullary reconstitution, painless palpation).
  • Treat vitamin D deficiency, osteoporosis, diabetes, thyroid disease.
  • Correct hindfoot varus, metatarsus adductus, cavus — risk factors for fracture, delayed union and refracture.
  • Athletes: operate.
Delayed / nonunion
Revision
  • Open the site, clear sclerotic canal, graft (calcaneal autograft, BMAC) and rigid IM compression.
  • Plantar (tension-side) plating is increasingly used, especially for revisions.
  • Correct varus with a medializing calcaneal osteotomy; cavus with a 1st MT dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy.
Dancer’s fracture
Distal spiral shaft
  • WBAT in cam walker or hard-soled shoe: pain-free walking 7.6, normal shoes 7.1, union 8.3 weeks; 9.1% delayed union, all healed by 6 months.
  • Fix displaced or comminuted oblique shaft fractures with small plates; minimal displacement may be fixed to keep the metatarsal parabola.

Use the largest solid screw that fits: diameter ≥4.5 mm (4.0–6.5 mm range), length about 64% and no more than 68–70% of metatarsal length — the 5th MT is curved, and a long screw distracts the fracture or perforates the cortex. Most isthmuses exceed 4.5 mm (81% of men, 74% of women).

Return to play

Elite athletes after fixation: union 96.7% at 9.1 weeks, 22.5% complications. Returning before 8 weeks after fixation was a significant risk factor for delayed complete union. Orthobiologics improved union but not return to play. AO: a single interfragmentary lag screw suffices for a single-plane fracture with good bone stock; most can be fixed percutaneously AO.

0–1 wk
Splint → cam walker
3 wk
PWB; swim, cycle
6 wk
Clinical + radiographic check
6–8 wk
Off crutches; physio
≥8 wk
Gradual return if healed

Sesamoid fracturesR&G 68

First line
Off-load 6–12 weeks
Forefoot off-loading shoe, cast or rocker-sole walker; slight plantarflexion to relax FHB. Symptomatic nonunion in up to 30%.
Fixation
Displaced / 2 large fragments
Percutaneous headless screw (athletes); 2.0-mm screws for two large fragments.
Excision
≥3 months failed care
Distal pole excision for unfixable displaced fragments; sesamoidectomy for painful nonunion or comminution. Never excise both.

Return to sport ~80% overall; conservative care as low as 64%. Sesamoidectomy gives the fastest return; fixation the best chance of full-level sport; fibular sesamoid fractures recover faster than tibial. After sesamoidectomy: 90% back to work by ~12 weeks, 80–94% return to sport.

Phalangeal fracturesR&G 68

The commonest forefoot injury; the fifth toe proximal phalanx is involved in ~30% and stubbing causes up to 75%. Most need only a stiff-soled shoe and buddy taping.

Nondisplaced
Stiff shoe 2–3 wk
Protected weight bearing and buddy taping, even if intra-articular.
Deformed
Closed reduction
Digital block, traction; pencil in the web space as a fulcrum for lesser toes. Judge by the clinical cascade and nail rotation, not the film.
Operative
Rare
Unstable hallux proximal/distal phalanx, persistent intra-articular step, open fracture → K-wires or mini-screws (2.0 plate described).
Nail bed
Treat as open
Fracture with nail bed bleeding or laceration: decompress, debride, repair.

High-energy "multiple injured foot"R&G 68

Damage control first: debridement, decompression, gross reduction, K-wires and an external fixator — then definitive fixation and coverage, usually at the end of the first week. Life before limb.

0–24 h
Acute care
I&D, fasciotomy, reduction, K-wires ± ex-fix.
24–72 h
Urgent revision
Second look at 24–48 h.
72–100 h
Early revision
Coverage within ~5 days in most; within 3 days lowered pre-flap infection (Liu).
>120 h
Delayed revision
Definitive fixation hindfoot → forefoot.

Zwipp sequence for definitive care: talus → ankle/pilon → calcaneus → Chopart → Lisfranc → metatarsals. Tibiocalcaneometatarsal external fixation gives the greatest three-plane stability.

Key point (Table 68-1)
TeamExperienced team; patient in the decision; functional rather than technical success
SalvageConstant reassessment of salvage vs primary amputation
BoneExternal fixator + K-wire transfixation
Soft tissueEarly, aggressive, serial debridement; early simultaneous bone and soft-tissue reconstruction
CoverageLiberal free muscle flaps, fibula flaps, bone grafts
RehabEarly intensive rehabilitation; gradual guarded weight bearing; education
Amputation predictors, NPWT and flap options
  • Amputation predictors (Working): number of fractured bones, all five metatarsals fractured, open dorsal/plantar injury, Gustilo grade, vascular injury, possibly complete loss of sensation. Jupiter: male sex, blunt trauma, associated fracture, crush or open wound.
  • NPWT: meta-analysis (2,780 patients) showed less infection than gauze; an RCT of 1,548 patients (Costa) showed no difference in deep infection.
  • Blisters: aspirate, deroof, silver sulfadiazine or nonadherent dressing; incisions through bloody blisters heal worse than through clear blisters.
  • Local flaps: distally based sural, EDB, FDB, medial plantar (instep), dorsalis pedis, lateral calcaneal, ADM. Free flaps: radial or lateral forearm, latissimus, rectus, serratus, gracilis (short pedicle).

Common set-upR&G 68

Almost every procedure in this chapter uses the same set-up: supine on a radiolucent table, bolster under the ipsilateral hip (contralateral hip for the 5th MT), fluoroscopy from the opposite side, thigh tourniquet, triangular cushion under the knee for plantigrade C-arm views, and small/mini-fragment sets plus an external fixator. AO positions supine with the knee flexed 90° AO.

TargetApproachProtect
NavicularDorsal longitudinal (talar neck → 2nd MT), just lateral to dorsalis pedis; ± medial between tibialis anterior and posteriorDorsalis pedis, peroneal nerve branches, EHL
CuboidLongitudinal dorsolateral over the cuboid, between 4th and 5th MT basesPeroneal tendons, sural nerve
TMT 1–3Dorsal, 1st–2nd web space from mid-diaphysis to TMT interval (extendable to talar head)Full-thickness flap over dorsalis pedis / deep peroneal nerve
TMT 3–5Second incision over the 4th MT to the cuboid; skin bridge ≥4–5 cmLateral cutaneous branch of the peroneal nerve
1st MTDorsolateral through the 1st intermetatarsal spaceDorsalis pedis, deep peroneal nerve, superficial peroneal branches
Central MTDorsal longitudinal over the boneSuperficial peroneal nerve
5th MT (IM screw)1–2 cm incision 2–3 cm proximal to the base, between peroneus brevis and longusSural nerve (~5 mm dorsal to the entry)

NavicularR&G 68

ORIF of a navicular body fractureStep walkthrough
Expose
  • Dorsal longitudinal incision, retract EHL and the neurovascular bundle.
  • Subperiosteal exposure, keeping soft-tissue attachments to large fragments.
  • L-shaped TN and/or NC arthrotomy; open the TN joint for comminution.
Step 1 / 6
Distract
  • Medial column distractor or external fixator: 2.5-mm Schanz pin medially in the talar neck perpendicular to its axis, second pin bicortical in the 1st MT base.
  • Not in the medial malleolus (small bone, poor vector).
  • Unstable lateral column too → calcaneal tuberosity to 5th MT base fixator, directly lateral.
Step 2 / 6
Reduce
  • Large fragments first; 1.25-mm K-wire joysticks; talar head and cuneiforms as articular templates.
  • Do not accept an articular step >1 mm.
  • Graft impacted voids (calcaneal tuberosity or distal medial tibia), then close cortical fragments over the graft.
Step 3 / 6
Fix
  • Simple split: two 2.7- or 3.5-mm screws (or screw + K-wire), countersunk in a trough.
  • Comminuted: mini-fragment (2.0 T, 2.7) or one-third/quarter tubular plate mediodorsally.
  • Restore the lateral corner — often under-addressed; shortening → abduction and arch collapse.
  • Never screw navicular to cuboid; transfixing cuneiforms (nonessential) is fine.
Step 4 / 6
Span if unstable
  • Internal bridge plate (2.0 semitubular or 2.7, 4–8 holes) anteromedially: talar head/neck → cuneiforms → 1st MT base.
  • Alignment check: a line from the talar neck bisecting the 1st MT–medial cuneiform joint.
  • Keep mild distraction; remove the plate across TN before unprotected weight bearing (~12 weeks).
Step 5 / 6
Check
  • Simulated weight-bearing views in three planes; dynamic fluoroscopy of the medial column.
  • Gross instability of essential joints → leave transarticular K-wires 6 weeks.
Step 6 / 6
Closed reduction technique (navicular)
  • Axial traction through the 1st toe to distract TN and NC joints.
  • K-wire joysticks; percutaneous pointed clamps on the split; provisional 1.6-mm wires.
  • Restore length with an external fixator; one or preferably two 2.7-mm low-profile or headless screws; washers in poor bone.
  • Any doubt about anatomic TN reduction → convert to ORIF.

CuboidR&G 68

  • Dorsolateral longitudinal incision centred on the cuboid; protect peroneal tendons and sural nerve; open CC and cuboid–metatarsal joints if involved.
  • Mini external fixator along the lateral column (1–2 pins in calcaneal tuberosity, 1 in 5th MT base) restores length and improves the view.
  • Lever main fragments against the intact adjacent surface; 1.25-mm K-wires; graft the defect; replace and buttress the lateral wall with a plate (mini X/H or precontoured, 2.0/2.7 bicortical).
  • Screw-only fixation is rare — the thin lateral cortex collapses. Do not transfix to navicular or cuneiforms.
  • Nondisplaced but ligamentously unstable: retrograde 1.6/2.0-mm K-wires from the 4th/5th MT bases into cuboid and lateral cuneiform, ± temporary CC transfixation.
Lateral spanning plate

2.7-mm reconstruction plate from the anterior calcaneal process to the 4th MT, crossing the cuboid, two screws in each bone; keep comminuted surfaces in mild distraction rather than compression; remove before unprotected weight bearing.

Lisfranc ORIFR&G 68 · AO

Open reduction and internal fixation of the TMT complexStep walkthrough
Decompress and expose
  • Measure compartment pressures; fasciotomy first if needed (plantar compartments via a separate medial incision).
  • Dorsal incision in the 1st–2nd web space; hooks on EHL/EHB; full-thickness flap over the bundle.
  • Debride joints of bony and ligamentous debris that block reduction.
Step 1 / 7
Tarsus first
  • Reduce unstable cuneiforms with a clamp; intercuneiform screws medial → lateral (two 2.7-mm screws give a stable medial block).
  • Reconstruct a displaced cuboid before the TMT line; distractor or ex-fix if the lateral column is short.
Step 2 / 7
Reduce the keystone
  • Traction on the 2nd ray with thumb counter-pressure; abduction–adduction maneuver for medial/lateral displacement.
  • A "pop" may be felt — confirm on fluoroscopy.
  • AO: an intramedullary K-wire in the 2nd MT can be used as a joystick and advanced into the middle cuneiform AO.
Step 3 / 7
Clamp and Lisfranc screw
  • Pointed clamp from the medial cuneiform to the lateral cortex of the 2nd MT base, in the vector of the Lisfranc ligament.
  • Retrograde provisional K-wire, then the Lisfranc screw (2.7/3.5 mm) from the medial cuneiform into the 2nd MT base, plus a retrograde 2.7-mm screw M2 → intermediate cuneiform.
  • Countersink; stay ≥5 mm from the joint line. Comminuted 2nd MT base → AO suggests an M1–M2 position screw instead AO.
Step 4 / 7
TMT-1, then TMT-3
  • Reduce TMT-1 to TMT-2; rule out rotation on simulated weight-bearing views.
  • Two crossing lag screws across TMT-1 (distal → proximal first).
  • TMT-3: retrograde 2.7-mm screw or small plate — may not need rigid fixation if TMT-4/5 are stable after TMT-1/2.
  • Base-of-2nd fracture: 1.5/2.0-mm screw dorsoplantar + Lisfranc screw distal to it, or a bridging plate.
Step 5 / 7
Lateral column
  • TMT-4/5 usually reduce with the medial column and move as one unit.
  • Fix with converging 1.6–2.0 mm K-wires into the cuboid; unstable 4th–5th interface → transverse lateral-to-medial blocking screw (2.7 or 3.5 mm).
  • Do not fuse — pseudarthrosis preferred.
Step 6 / 7
Unreconstructable
  • Comminution: 2.7-mm reconstruction bridge plate medially (talar head/navicular or cuneiform → 1st MT), two screws each end; lateral from anterior calcaneal process to 4th MT.
  • Joint involvement >25% → primary arthrodesis of TMT 1–3.
  • Shorten or remove plates crossing TN before weight bearing.
Step 7 / 7
Primary arthrodesis of TMT 1–3 — key steps
  • Stabilize the cuneiforms first; reduce TMT-2, then TMT-1, then TMT-3 (others start with TMT-1).
  • Medial distractor (Schanz pins in medial cuneiform or talus and 1st MT base); denude cartilage with curettes and osteotomes, perforate subchondral bone with a 1.25-mm wire or 1.6-mm drill — no saw (shortening).
  • TMT-1 is oval, ~30 mm dorsoplantar: missed plantar/lateral cartilage leaves dorsal and varus malalignment; avoid rotation.
  • Crossed 2.7/3.5-mm lag screws (trough for the retrograde screw) or a 2.7/Lapidus plate proximal → distal; graft gaps (local, distal tibia, calcaneus).
  • TMT-4/5: no fusion — temporary 1.6/2.0-mm K-wires to the cuboid.
Closed reduction and percutaneous fixation (CRIF)
  • Axial traction via the 1st toe or finger traps; percutaneous clamp on the 2nd MT base; 1.25/1.6-mm wires.
  • At least one, ideally two 2.7-mm (or 3.5-mm) low-profile screws; washers; transfix to cuboid or cuneiforms if needed.
  • Stable after closed reduction and no other operative injury → treat nonoperatively. TMT arthroscopy can help delayed cases.

MetatarsalsR&G 68

Antegrade–retrograde K-wire fixation of a central MT fractureStep walkthrough
Expose
  • Stab or short dorsal incision just proximal to the fracture (open if needed); curette the fracture ends.
Step 1 / 4
Antegrade
  • Drive a smooth wire distally down the shaft of the distal fragment.
Step 2 / 4
Exit plantar
  • Hold the MTP reduced so the wire passes through the joint and engages the plantar cortex of the proximal phalanx, out through the plantar skin.
  • Chuck the distal end and back the wire out until it clears the fracture.
Step 3 / 4
Retrograde
  • Reduce the fracture and drive the wire back across it into the proximal fragment (into the cuneiform or cuboid for base fractures).
  • Remove at 6–8 weeks once callus is visible.
Step 4 / 4
Intramedullary screw for a proximal 5th MT fractureStep walkthrough
Mark
  • Fluoroscopic AP: draw the 5th MT axis on the dorsum; lateral: draw it on the side.
  • Incision 2–3 cm proximal to the base, midway between the two lines; 1–2 cm long.
Step 1 / 4
Entry
  • Between peroneus brevis and longus; protect the sural nerve (~5 mm dorsal).
  • Guidewire "high and inside" at the lateral cartilage margin — ~1 cm dorsal to the inferior tuberosity margin, just medial to the peroneus brevis insertion, angled ~7° off the sole with the ankle neutral.
Step 2 / 4
Prepare
  • Nonunion/delayed union: open the site, rongeur/osteotome, clear the sclerotic canal, pack autograft (e.g., calcaneal).
  • Estimate diameter on AP and length on lateral preoperatively.
Step 3 / 4
Screw
  • Solid or cannulated compression screw ≥4.5 mm, tightly filling the canal, length ~64% (≤68–70%) of the MT.
  • Threads just past the fracture; avoid distraction from overlength, no tapping, interposition or rotational torque.
  • Screw must engage distal cortex without distorting alignment (unicortical gapping → bunionette, delayed healing).
Step 4 / 4

SesamoidsR&G 68

Percutaneous
Headless screw
Hallux in maximal dorsiflexion; stab incision distally; 1-mm wire along axial and lateral mid-diameter; 2-mm cannulated drill; headless screw distal → proximal, distal thread buried.
Medial sesamoidectomy
Medial approach
3–4 cm incision; protect the plantar digital nerve; capsulotomy below abductor hallucis; preserve FHB; transfer abductor hallucis into the defect; watertight capsule.
Lateral sesamoidectomy
Dorsal 1st web
Divide the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament; protect the common digital nerve; detach and repair adductor hallucis; spare FHL. Plantar approach avoided (scar, keratosis).

Foot fasciotomyR&G 68

  • Three incisions (dorsomedial, dorsolateral, medial) release all 9–10 compartments including the deep calcaneal. Skin bridge ≥3 cm between dorsal incisions.
  • A medial midfoot incision gave the fastest pressure fall in all compartments including the tarsal tunnel; single or double dorsal incisions did not match it.
  • Usually no tourniquet. Recheck pressures intraoperatively; if still raised, check the intermediate (calcaneal) compartment release.
  • Second look at 12–48 h; skin traction/dermatotraction; closure or graft/flap at 5–7 days. Unstable fractures: temporary K-wires/2.7-mm screws + ex-fix first.

OverviewR&G 68

Early problems are soft-tissue driven (wounds, infection, compartment syndrome); late problems are posttraumatic arthritis, column shortening with deformity, and implant irritation.

InjuryCommon adverse outcomes
NavicularTN arthritis, wound infection, chronic pain (arthritis, implants, neuromas), nonunion/malunion, osteonecrosis, DVT, pes planus or cavus
CuboidCC and CMT arthritis, infection, chronic pain, nonunion/malunion, pes planus, abduction, cavus, DVT
CuneiformChronic pain, secondary dislocation after nonoperative care, nonunion, arch collapse
TMTCompartment syndrome, wound problems, posttraumatic OA, delayed/nonunion, pain, hardware problems, stiffness, instability, deformity
1st MTShortening, rotation, malalignment of the head
Central MTMalalignment, delayed union, claw toes after compartment syndrome, DVT
5th MTProminent screw head, distal cortical penetration, delayed union, refracture, deformity, chronic low-grade pain
SesamoidStiffness, digital nerve injury, hallux valgus (medial excision), hallux varus/metatarsalgia (lateral), cock-up toe (both excised)

Midfoot sequelaeR&G 68

Navicular
Arthritis dominates
Sangeorzan: fair/poor results incl. pain in one-third; no residual disability in only 19%. Coulibaly: pes planus 21%, pes cavus 26%.
Navicular nonunion
Rare
Commoner in severe types; bone graft + fixation if length is correct; collapsed first ray needs medial column lengthening or opening-wedge osteotomy.
Cuboid
Lateral column shortening
Pes planus 17%, pes cavus 18%; midtarsal subluxation with CC compromise → arthritis in 80%.
Soft tissue
Thin envelope
Local flaps and grafts are poor choices on the foot; thin free flaps (parascapular, lateral thigh) give good coverage.

Lateral column shortening → midfoot abduction and flatfoot. Correct with a lengthening osteotomy of the cuboid or CC joint with tricortical iliac graft; if the CC joint is arthritic, CC distraction arthrodesis — lengthening through cuboid or calcaneus preserves CC motion.

  • Painful CC arthritis → CC arthrodesis (debride, iliac graft, small H-plate).
  • Severe CMT-4/5 arthritis → interposition arthroplasty, not fusion.
  • Even after arthrodesis, most navicular patients keep pain and need shoe support.
  • Monitor on standing films: talometatarsal angles, calcaneal pitch, navicular/cuboid height, TN coverage, column lengths.

Tarsometatarsal sequelaeR&G 68

  • Secondary OA is the commonest sequela after both nonoperative and operative care; radiographic severity correlates poorly with disability. Secondary arthrodesis is an effective salvage.
  • Wilson: vascular compromise of the toes in 3 of 20. Loss of the medial longitudinal arch correlated with poor outcome in pure ligamentous injuries.
  • Delay in treatment and work-related injury significantly reduce outcomes; fewer secondary operations after PA than ORIF (Henning).
  • Subtle injuries followed nonoperatively developed midfoot arthritis in 40% — assess them thoroughly.

Forefoot sequelaeR&G 68

1st MT
Load imbalance
Half the forefoot load passes through MT-1/2; shortening or rotation causes MTP and medial column pain and gait change.
Central MT
Head malposition
Plantarflexed head → intractable plantar keratosis; symptomatic deformity → simple osteotomy. IM wiring can necrose the plantar fat pad; superficial peroneal nerve injury → causalgia.
Central MT
Delayed union
Metaphyseal nonunion is uncommon; graft or LIPUS may help. Overlong central MT → more stress fractures.
5th MT
Surgical failure
Early return, wrong screw angle or size, inadequate graft or incomplete debridement of the sclerotic canal.
  • Zone 1 nonunion is usually asymptomatic; painful small fragments are excised; large fragments including the peroneus brevis insertion → graft + 3.5/4.0-mm lag screw or hook plate.
  • Chronic low-level pain in up to 30% at 1 year after 5th MT fracture, but <10% limit activity.
  • Phalanges: malalignment → shoe problems and soft corns; nonunited chips excised; painful malunion or arthritis → arthrodesis or resection arthroplasty.

Compartment syndrome of the footR&G 68

An absolute emergency. Clinical signs are unreliable (sensitivity 13–19% in the leg), so measure pressures whenever suspicion exists.

>30mm Hg absolute
<30mm Hg below diastolic (ΔP)
~2%of isolated foot injuries fasciotomized
~2×risk with crush
up to 20%from low-energy injuries
Causes
Crush, Lisfranc, calcaneus
Also after ankle ORIF, exertion and reperfusion. One-third in isolated forefoot injuries; forefoot + midfoot combined is a risk factor.
Pathophysiology
Pressure-dependent ischemia
≥30 mm Hg for 8 hours causes significant muscle necrosis (Hargens); one compartment’s pressure rise raises all others with intact skin.
Impending
Release dressings
Split and spread casts and padding; slight elevation; re-examine clinically and invasively. No role for nonoperative care once established.
Late
Claw toes
Contractures and claw toes, mainly from the interosseous compartments in forefoot injury.
Fasciotomy indications
  • Clinical suspicion: intractable pain, pain on passive stretch.
  • Pressure >30 mm Hg, or <30 mm Hg below diastolic, or <30–40 mm Hg below MAP.
  • The crushed foot; the multiple injured foot.
